**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 103, verses 1–3 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿By time﴾ [1] ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [2] ﴿Except for those who have believed and done righteous deeds and advised each other to truth and advised each other to patience﴾ [3].

God Most High swears by *al-ʿAṣr* (time), an oath intended to emphasize the statement, as is the custom of the oaths in the Qur'an.

The thing sworn by is among the manifestations of the wondrous creation of the Lord, which points to the greatness of His power and the breadth of His knowledge.

The word *al-ʿAṣr* has several meanings. The one intended here must be a state indicating an attribute of God's acts. It is determined either by its being attached to something that is implied, or by the context, or by a known reference. Whatever is meant here, the oath by it, insofar as it is a period of time, reminds one of the great power of God Most High in creating the world and its conditions, and of great and blessed matters, such as the specific prayer, or a particular blessed age.

The most common usage of the word *ʿAṣr* is that it is a proper name by predominance for a certain time, between the end of the time of *Ẓuhr* and the yellowing of the sun [*iṣfirār al-shams*]. Its beginning is when the shadow of an object becomes equal to the object itself, after the length it had at the sun's zenith, and it extends until the shadow of the object becomes twice its length, after the shadow it had at the sun's zenith. That is the time of the sun's yellowing, and *ʿAṣr* is the beginning of the evening (*ʿashiyy*). It is followed by *al-Aṣīl* and reddening, which is what precedes the sunset. Al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥillizah said:

*She was startled by a sound, and the hunter frightened her at the time of ʿAṣr, when the evening had drawn near.*

That time signals the approaching end of the day, and it reminds one of the creation of the sun and the earth, and the system of the earth's movement around the sun, which is the movement from which night and day are formed every day. In this respect it is like the oath by *al-Ḍuḥā*, by night and day, and by dawn, among the atmospheric conditions that change with the change in the direction of the sun's rays toward the terrestrial sphere.

At that time people prepare to disengage from their work during the day, such as tending their fields and gardens, and their trade in their markets. It thus reminds one of the wisdom in the system of human society, and of what God inspired in human nature of persistence in work, and of a system for its beginning and its ending. At that time people are stirred to return to their homes to spend the night and to enjoy the company of their families and children. It is also among the blessings or the bounties, and it contains an allusion to reminding one of life itself, when people's appointed terms draw near after the passing of the stages of youth, middle age, and old age.

Defining it with the definite article in these respects is the definition of the mental reference (*al-ʿahd al-dhihnī*), i.e., every age.

*Al-ʿAṣr* is also applied to the prayer timed to the time of ʿAṣr, and it is a highly esteemed prayer. It has been said that it is what is meant by "the middle" in God's words: ﴿Guard the prayers, and the middle prayer﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 238]. It has come in a hadith: ("Whoever misses the ʿAṣr prayer, it is as if he has been robbed of his family and his property"). And it is reported in a sound hadith: ("Three whom God will not speak to on the Day of Resurrection") and he mentioned: ("and a man who swore a false oath after ʿAṣr over a commodity, for which he was given what he was not given"). Its definition in this sense is the definition of the known reference, and it became a proper name by predominance, as is the case with many nouns of kind defined by the definite article, such as *al-ʿAqabah*.

*Al-ʿAṣr* is also applied to a known period for the existence of a generation of people, or a king, or a prophet, or a religion, and it is specified by annexation, so one says: "the age of Fiṭḥal," "the age of Ibrahim," "the age of Alexander," "the Age of Ignorance." It is possible that this sense is intended here, and that the one meant is the age of the Prophet (ﷺ). The definition here is the definition of the presential reference (*al-ʿahd al-ḥuḍūrī*), like the definition in "the day" in your saying: "I did such-and-such today." So the oath by it is like the oath by his life in God's words: (By your life) [al-Ḥijr: 72]. Al-Fakhr said: "He, Exalted is He, swore by His time in this verse, by His place in His words: ﴿And you are a resident of this city﴾ [al-Balad: 2], and by His life in His words: (By your life). [End of quotation]."

It is also possible that the age of Islam as a whole is meant, which is the final of the ages of the religions for this world. The Prophet (ﷺ) likened the age of the Muslim community, relative to the age of the Jews and the age of the Christians, to the time after the ʿAṣr prayer until sunset, saying: ("The example of the Muslims, the Jews, and the Christians is like a man who hired workers to work for him until night. The Jews worked until midday, then they said: 'We have no need for your wage, and what we did is void.' He hired others after them and said: 'Complete the rest of your day, and you will have what I stipulated for them.' They worked until the time of the ʿAṣr prayer, then they said: 'What we did is void for you, and you will have the wage that you set for us.' He hired a group to work the rest of their day, and they worked until the sun set, and they completed the wage of both groups. So you are they"). Perhaps that prophetic parable is connected to an allusion to the age of Islam in this verse.

It is also possible that *al-ʿAṣr* in this verse is interpreted as the whole of time. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "Ubayy ibn Kaʿb said: 'I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about al-ʿAṣr, and he said: "Your Lord swore by the end of the day."'" These meanings are not all covered by the word *al-ʿAṣr* except by its possible senses.

The connection of the oath by *al-ʿAṣr* to the purpose of the surah, if the age of Islam is intended, is evident, for it explains the condition of people in the age of Islam, between those who disbelieved in it and those who believed and fulfilled their share of the works that Islam brought, and from it one knows the condition of those who embraced Islam but whose works had varying degrees of shortcoming. As for the conditions of the nations that existed before Islam, they were varied according to whether prophets came to some nations, and whether some nations remained without laws, adhering to other than the religion of Islam, such as polytheism, or to a religion whose abrogation Islam brought, such as Judaism and Christianity. God Most High said: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him, and he will be among the losers in the Hereafter﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 85], in the Surah of Āl ʿImrān.

The definition of *al-insān* (mankind) is the definition of the kind, intended to include all, and this is a customary inclusion, because it encompasses the individuals of the human species existing at the time of the revelation of the verse, which is the time of the rise of Islam, as you have learned shortly before. It is restricted to the people whom the call reached across the world's lands, with variation among them. When an exception was made from it of those who believed and did righteous deeds, its ruling remained valid for non-believers, as will come later...

*Al-khusr* (loss) is a verbal noun, and it is the opposite of profit in trade. It is used here metaphorically for bad outcome, for whoever thinks that he has a good outcome, and that is the lasting outcome, which is the outcome of a person in his afterlife, whether bliss or punishment.

This was discussed in God's words: ﴿So their trade did not profit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16] in Surah al-Baqarah, and its like recurs in the Qur'an, both nearby and far.

The expression of *fī* (in) in His words: ﴿is in loss﴾ is metaphorical; it compares the constant accompaniment of loss to the encompassing of the container by the contained, and so it is more eloquent than saying: "Indeed mankind is a loser."

The coming of this statement in generality, along with its emphasis by the oath and the emphatic particle in its answer, conveys awe and warning about the state that encompasses most people.

It is followed by the exception in His words: ﴿Except for those who have believed﴾ and the verse continues. Thus the ruling is fully established in the hearer's mind, showing that people are of two groups: a group that is overtaken by loss, and a group to which no part of it applies. Those who believed and did righteous deeds, loss does not overtake them in any way, provided they do not abandon any of the righteous deeds by committing their opposites, which are the evil deeds.

Among the greatest righteous deeds is repentance from sins for those who commit them. Whoever is characterized by faith and did not commit evil deeds, or committed them and repented of them, the opposite of loss is realized for him, which is metaphorical profit, i.e., the good outcome of his affair. As for whoever does not do righteous deeds and does not repent of his evil deeds, the ruling of the excepted group, which is loss, is realized in him.

This loss varies: its greatest and most enduring form is the loss that results from the absence of faith in God's oneness and in the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ). Other than that, the degrees of loss vary according to the abundance of evil deeds, both outward and inward. What Islam determined for these degrees of deeds, including the forgiveness of some minor faults (*lamam*) when their doer avoids major sins and grave transgressions, is what God Most High's words were interpreted as: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds﴾ [Hūd: 114].

This statement is meant to refer to what happens in the future, by the context of warning and threat, i.e., "indeed they are in loss" in the eternal, everlasting afterlife. So there is no regard for people's conditions in the present life. God Most High said: ﴿Let not the strutting of those who disbelieve throughout the land deceive you﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 196] ﴿A brief enjoyment, then their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 197].

The indefiniteness of (*khusr*, loss) may be for variety (i.e., various kinds of loss), and it may be for magnification and generalization in a context of awe and in the context of an oath.

The meaning: indeed, people are in great loss, and they are the polytheists.

The definite article in His words (*al-ṣāliḥāt*, the righteous deeds) is the definition of the kind, intended to include all, i.e., they did all the righteous deeds that they were commanded to perform by the command of the religion. Doing righteous deeds includes abandoning evil deeds. The exception of those characterized by the content of the relative clause and its conjunction indicates the reason for the ruling of the exception, which is the opposite of the ruling established for the excepted group. Indeed, they are not in loss because they believed and did righteous deeds.

As for faith, it is a reality that is predicated of its particulars univocally (*bi-l-tawāṭuʾ*), whereas the generality of righteous deeds is predicated of it by gradation (*bi-l-tashakkuk*). This indicates that the absence of loss from them is measured in proportion to the righteous deeds they performed, and there are many degrees in that.

The exception of those who believed and did righteous deeds from being in loss shows that the cause of the rest of humanity being in loss is the absence of faith and righteous deed, by the indication of the implication of the attribute (*mafhūm al-ṣifa*). It is known from the relative clause that faith and righteous deed are the cause of the absence of loss enveloping a person.

Mutual exhortation to truth and mutual exhortation to patience are conjoined to the doing of righteous deeds, even though they are themselves part of righteous deeds. This is the conjunction of the particular to the general, for the sake of emphasis on it. Because it may be overlooked, one might suppose that righteous deed is what one's own deed affects one's own person, so attention is drawn to the fact that among the deeds commanded is guiding a Muslim to others and calling them to truth. Thus mutual exhortation to truth includes teaching the realities of guidance and the tenets of correct belief, and training the soul to understand them by doing what is good and abandoning what is wrong.

Mutual exhortation to patience is conjoined to mutual exhortation to truth as a conjunction of the particular to the general too, even though its particularity is particular from one aspect, because patience is bearing the hardship of establishing the truth and the harm that a Muslim encounters in himself in establishing some of the truth.

The reality of patience is: a person restraining himself from obtaining what he desires, or from attempting to obtain it (if it is difficult to obtain), so he abandons the attempt to obtain it out of fear of harm that would result from taking it, such as fear of God's anger or the punishment of rulers, or out of desire to gain benefit from it, such as patience upon the hardship of jihad and hajj seeking reward, and patience upon arduous works seeking wealth, fame, or the like.

Among patience is bearing what a Muslim encounters when he enjoins good, such as the displeasure of some of those he commands, or their harm by speech, such as one who says to the one commanding him: "Why don't you look to your own affairs?" or the like.

As for enduring the hardship of committing forbidden acts, such as patience in enduring the strain of staying up late in idle play and sins, and patience in enduring the foulness of the taste of wine for its drinker, this is not patience, because that endurance arises from a preponderance of desire for that hardship over the aversion to the hardship that would confront him in abandoning it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 103, verse 1–3 (part 2 of 2):

The Almighty's words ﴿and they enjoin one another to the truth, and they enjoin one another to patience﴾ encompass the establishment of all the religious interests. Thus, the Islamic creeds and the religious ethics are included in "the truth," and the righteous deeds and the avoidance of evil deeds are included in "patience."

Acquiring patience (sabr) is the foundation (milak) of all virtuous character traits, for training oneself in praiseworthy ethics cannot be free of compelling oneself to oppose many desires. Opposing them involves hardship, which requires patience in bearing it, until noble character becomes an acquired disposition (malakah) for the one who disciplines his soul in it, as 'Amr ibn al-'As said:

*When a man does not abandon a food he loves,
and does not restrain a misguided heart wherever it turns,
Then it is near that over time he will be found to have a disgrace,
which, whenever its like is mentioned, fills the mouths.*

[Page 534]

Likewise, all righteous deeds cannot be free of forcing the soul to abandon what it inclines toward. In a hadith: "The Garden is surrounded by hardships, and the Fire is surrounded by desires." And from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib: "Patience is a riding beast that does not stumble."

The discussion of patience has already been dealt with in full detail at the Almighty's words ﴿and seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45] in Surah al-Baqarah.

The form of the verb "enjoining one another" (al-tawasi) to the truth and to patience indicates that the condition of believers' life should be based on the widespread mutual exhortation to these two as a constant practice among them. This requires that believers be characterized by upholding the truth and by patiently enduring hardships in the interests of Islam and its community, because of the customary understanding among people that no one enjoins another to persist in a matter unless he himself sees that matter as worthy of persistence, since it is rare for anyone to undertake to command something truthful that he himself does not do, or to command patience while he himself is impatient. The Almighty has said, rebuking the Children of Israel: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people while you forget yourselves, and you recite the Scripture? Will you not reason?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 44]. This meaning has already been mentioned at the Almighty's words ﴿and you do not urge one another to feed the poor﴾ [al-Fajr: 18] in Surah al-Fajr.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Surah al-Humazah

This surah is named in the mushafs and most tafsir works "Surat al-Humazah" (the Surah of the Backbiter) with the definite article. In Sahih al-Bukhari and some tafsir works it is titled "Surat Waylun li-kulli Humazah" (the Surah of "Woe to every backbiter"). Al-Firuzabadi, in Basa'ir dhawi al-tamyiz, mentioned that it is also called "Surat al-Hutamah" (the Surah of the Crusher), because this word occurs in it.

It is Meccan (makkiyyah, revealed before the Hijrah) by consensus.

It is counted as the thirty-second in the order of the surahs' revelation. It was revealed after Surat al-Qiyamah and before Surat al-Mursalat.

Its verses number nine by consensus.

It is narrated that it was revealed concerning a group of polytheists who had set themselves up to slander and abuse the Muslims and to fabricate evil reports about them. Among these polytheists named were al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah al-Makhzumi, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, Ubayy ibn Khalaf, Jamil ibn Ma'mar of the Banu Jumah (this one embraced Islam on the day of the Conquest and witnessed Hunayn), and al-'As ibn Wa'il of the Banu Sahm. All of them were among the chiefs of Quraysh. Also named were al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth and al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, the two of the Thaqif, chiefs of Thaqif from the people of al-Ta'if. All of these were people of wealth in the pre-Islamic period, and prosperous with their riches and their leadership. The verse of the surah came in general terms, so its ruling encompassed those named and whoever was of their kind among the polytheists, and their names were not mentioned.

* * *

The purpose of this surah is the warning to a group of polytheists who made the slandering and defaming of the Muslims a form of their harms, hoping that the weariness caused by the varieties of harm would compel them to turn away from Islam and return to polytheism.

Mutual exhortation to patience is conjoined to mutual exhortation to truth as a conjunction of the particular to the general too, even though its particularity is particular from one aspect, because patience is bearing the hardship of establishing the truth and the harm that a Muslim encounters in himself in establishing some of the truth.

The reality of patience is: a person restraining himself from obtaining what he desires, or from attempting to obtain it (if it is difficult to obtain), so he abandons the attempt to obtain it out of fear of harm that would result from taking it, such as fear of God's anger or the punishment of rulers, or out of desire to gain benefit from it, such as patience upon the hardship of jihad and hajj seeking reward, and patience upon arduous works seeking wealth, fame, or the like.

Among patience is bearing what a Muslim encounters when he enjoins good, such as the displeasure of some of those he commands, or their harm by speech, such as one who says to the one commanding him: "Why don't you look to your own affairs?" or the like.

As for enduring the hardship of committing forbidden acts, such as patience in enduring the strain of staying up late in idle play and sins, and patience in enduring the foulness of the taste of wine for its drinker, this is not patience, because that endurance arises from a preponderance of desire for that hardship over the aversion to the hardship that would confront him in abandoning it.

The Almighty's words ﴿and they enjoin one another to the truth, and they enjoin one another to patience﴾ encompass the establishment of all the religious interests. Thus, the Islamic creeds and the religious ethics are included in "the truth," and the righteous deeds and the avoidance of evil deeds are included in "patience."

Acquiring patience (sabr) is the foundation (milak) of all virtuous character traits, for training oneself in praiseworthy ethics cannot be free of compelling oneself to oppose many desires. Opposing them involves hardship, which requires patience in bearing it, until noble character becomes an acquired disposition (malakah) for the one who disciplines his soul in it, as 'Amr ibn al-'As said:

*When a man does not abandon a food he loves,
and does not restrain a misguided heart wherever it turns,
Then it is near that over time he will be found to have a disgrace,
which, whenever its like is mentioned, fills the mouths.*

[Page 534]

Likewise, all righteous deeds cannot be free of forcing the soul to abandon what it inclines toward. In a hadith: "The Garden is surrounded by hardships, and the Fire is surrounded by desires." And from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib: "Patience is a riding beast that does not stumble."

The discussion of patience has already been dealt with in full detail at the Almighty's words ﴿and seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45] in Surah al-Baqarah.

The form of the verb "enjoining one another" (al-tawasi) to the truth and to patience indicates that the condition of believers' life should be based on the widespread mutual exhortation to these two as a constant practice among them. This requires that believers be characterized by upholding the truth and by patiently enduring hardships in the interests of Islam and its community, because of the customary understanding among people that no one enjoins another to persist in a matter unless he himself sees that matter as worthy of persistence, since it is rare for anyone to undertake to command something truthful that he himself does not do, or to command patience while he himself is impatient. The Almighty has said, rebuking the Children of Israel: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people while you forget yourselves, and you recite the Scripture? Will you not reason?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 44]. Surah al-Humazah

* * *

The purpose of this surah is the warning to a group of polytheists who made the slandering and defaming of the Muslims a form of their harms, hoping that the weariness caused by the varieties of harm would compel them to turn away from Islam and return to polytheism.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 103, verses 1–3 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿By time﴾ [1] ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [2] ﴿Except for those who have believed and done righteous deeds and advised each other to truth and advised each other to patience﴾ [3].

God Most High swears by *al-ʿAṣr* (time), an oath intended to emphasize the statement, as is the custom of the oaths in the Qur'an.

The thing sworn by is among the manifestations of the wondrous creation of the Lord, which points to the greatness of His power and the breadth of His knowledge.

The word *al-ʿAṣr* has several meanings. The one intended here must be a state indicating an attribute of God's acts. It is determined either by its being attached to something that is implied, or by the context, or by a known reference. Whatever is meant here, the oath by it, insofar as it is a period of time, reminds one of the great power of God Most High in creating the world and its conditions, and of great and blessed matters, such as the specific prayer, or a particular blessed age.

The most common usage of the word *ʿAṣr* is that it is a proper name by predominance for a certain time, between the end of the time of *Ẓuhr* and the yellowing of the sun [*iṣfirār al-shams*]. Its beginning is when the shadow of an object becomes equal to the object itself, after the length it had at the sun's zenith, and it extends until the shadow of the object becomes twice its length, after the shadow it had at the sun's zenith. That is the time of the sun's yellowing, and *ʿAṣr* is the beginning of the evening (*ʿashiyy*). It is followed by *al-Aṣīl* and reddening, which is what precedes the sunset. Al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥillizah said:

*She was startled by a sound, and the hunter frightened her at the time of ʿAṣr, when the evening had drawn near.*

That time signals the approaching end of the day, and it reminds one of the creation of the sun and the earth, and the system of the earth's movement around the sun, which is the movement from which night and day are formed every day. In this respect it is like the oath by *al-Ḍuḥā*, by night and day, and by dawn, among the atmospheric conditions that change with the change in the direction of the sun's rays toward the terrestrial sphere.

At that time people prepare to disengage from their work during the day, such as tending their fields and gardens, and their trade in their markets. It thus reminds one of the wisdom in the system of human society, and of what God inspired in human nature of persistence in work, and of a system for its beginning and its ending. At that time people are stirred to return to their homes to spend the night and to enjoy the company of their families and children. It is also among the blessings or the bounties, and it contains an allusion to reminding one of life itself, when people's appointed terms draw near after the passing of the stages of youth, middle age, and old age.

Defining it with the definite article in these respects is the definition of the mental reference (*al-ʿahd al-dhihnī*), i.e., every age.

*Al-ʿAṣr* is also applied to the prayer timed to the time of ʿAṣr, and it is a highly esteemed prayer. It has been said that it is what is meant by "the middle" in God's words: ﴿Guard the prayers, and the middle prayer﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 238]. It has come in a hadith: ("Whoever misses the ʿAṣr prayer, it is as if he has been robbed of his family and his property"). And it is reported in a sound hadith: ("Three whom God will not speak to on the Day of Resurrection") and he mentioned: ("and a man who swore a false oath after ʿAṣr over a commodity, for which he was given what he was not given"). Its definition in this sense is the definition of the known reference, and it became a proper name by predominance, as is the case with many nouns of kind defined by the definite article, such as *al-ʿAqabah*.

*Al-ʿAṣr* is also applied to a known period for the existence of a generation of people, or a king, or a prophet, or a religion, and it is specified by annexation, so one says: "the age of Fiṭḥal," "the age of Ibrahim," "the age of Alexander," "the Age of Ignorance." It is possible that this sense is intended here, and that the one meant is the age of the Prophet (ﷺ). The definition here is the definition of the presential reference (*al-ʿahd al-ḥuḍūrī*), like the definition in "the day" in your saying: "I did such-and-such today." So the oath by it is like the oath by his life in God's words: (By your life) [al-Ḥijr: 72]. Al-Fakhr said: "He, Exalted is He, swore by His time in this verse, by His place in His words: ﴿And you are a resident of this city﴾ [al-Balad: 2], and by His life in His words: (By your life). [End of quotation]."

It is also possible that the age of Islam as a whole is meant, which is the final of the ages of the religions for this world. The Prophet (ﷺ) likened the age of the Muslim community, relative to the age of the Jews and the age of the Christians, to the time after the ʿAṣr prayer until sunset, saying: ("The example of the Muslims, the Jews, and the Christians is like a man who hired workers to work for him until night. The Jews worked until midday, then they said: 'We have no need for your wage, and what we did is void.' He hired others after them and said: 'Complete the rest of your day, and you will have what I stipulated for them.' They worked until the time of the ʿAṣr prayer, then they said: 'What we did is void for you, and you will have the wage that you set for us.' He hired a group to work the rest of their day, and they worked until the sun set, and they completed the wage of both groups. So you are they"). Perhaps that prophetic parable is connected to an allusion to the age of Islam in this verse.

It is also possible that *al-ʿAṣr* in this verse is interpreted as the whole of time. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "Ubayy ibn Kaʿb said: 'I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about al-ʿAṣr, and he said: "Your Lord swore by the end of the day."'" These meanings are not all covered by the word *al-ʿAṣr* except by its possible senses.

The connection of the oath by *al-ʿAṣr* to the purpose of the surah, if the age of Islam is intended, is evident, for it explains the condition of people in the age of Islam, between those who disbelieved in it and those who believed and fulfilled their share of the works that Islam brought, and from it one knows the condition of those who embraced Islam but whose works had varying degrees of shortcoming. As for the conditions of the nations that existed before Islam, they were varied according to whether prophets came to some nations, and whether some nations remained without laws, adhering to other than the religion of Islam, such as polytheism, or to a religion whose abrogation Islam brought, such as Judaism and Christianity. God Most High said: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him, and he will be among the losers in the Hereafter﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 85], in the Surah of Āl ʿImrān.

The definition of *al-insān* (mankind) is the definition of the kind, intended to include all, and this is a customary inclusion, because it encompasses the individuals of the human species existing at the time of the revelation of the verse, which is the time of the rise of Islam, as you have learned shortly before. It is restricted to the people whom the call reached across the world's lands, with variation among them. When an exception was made from it of those who believed and did righteous deeds, its ruling remained valid for non-believers, as will come later...

*Al-khusr* (loss) is a verbal noun, and it is the opposite of profit in trade. It is used here metaphorically for bad outcome, for whoever thinks that he has a good outcome, and that is the lasting outcome, which is the outcome of a person in his afterlife, whether bliss or punishment.

This was discussed in God's words: ﴿So their trade did not profit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16] in Surah al-Baqarah, and its like recurs in the Qur'an, both nearby and far.

The expression of *fī* (in) in His words: ﴿is in loss﴾ is metaphorical; it compares the constant accompaniment of loss to the encompassing of the container by the contained, and so it is more eloquent than saying: "Indeed mankind is a loser."

The coming of this statement in generality, along with its emphasis by the oath and the emphatic particle in its answer, conveys awe and warning about the state that encompasses most people.

It is followed by the exception in His words: ﴿Except for those who have believed﴾ and the verse continues. Thus the ruling is fully established in the hearer's mind, showing that people are of two groups: a group that is overtaken by loss, and a group to which no part of it applies. Those who believed and did righteous deeds, loss does not overtake them in any way, provided they do not abandon any of the righteous deeds by committing their opposites, which are the evil deeds.

Among the greatest righteous deeds is repentance from sins for those who commit them. Whoever is characterized by faith and did not commit evil deeds, or committed them and repented of them, the opposite of loss is realized for him, which is metaphorical profit, i.e., the good outcome of his affair. As for whoever does not do righteous deeds and does not repent of his evil deeds, the ruling of the excepted group, which is loss, is realized in him.

This loss varies: its greatest and most enduring form is the loss that results from the absence of faith in God's oneness and in the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ). Other than that, the degrees of loss vary according to the abundance of evil deeds, both outward and inward. What Islam determined for these degrees of deeds, including the forgiveness of some minor faults (*lamam*) when their doer avoids major sins and grave transgressions, is what God Most High's words were interpreted as: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds﴾ [Hūd: 114].

This statement is meant to refer to what happens in the future, by the context of warning and threat, i.e., "indeed they are in loss" in the eternal, everlasting afterlife. So there is no regard for people's conditions in the present life. God Most High said: ﴿Let not the strutting of those who disbelieve throughout the land deceive you﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 196] ﴿A brief enjoyment, then their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 197].

The indefiniteness of (*khusr*, loss) may be for variety (i.e., various kinds of loss), and it may be for magnification and generalization in a context of awe and in the context of an oath.

The meaning: indeed, people are in great loss, and they are the polytheists.

The definite article in His words (*al-ṣāliḥāt*, the righteous deeds) is the definition of the kind, intended to include all, i.e., they did all the righteous deeds that they were commanded to perform by the command of the religion. Doing righteous deeds includes abandoning evil deeds. The exception of those characterized by the content of the relative clause and its conjunction indicates the reason for the ruling of the exception, which is the opposite of the ruling established for the excepted group. Indeed, they are not in loss because they believed and did righteous deeds.

As for faith, it is a reality that is predicated of its particulars univocally (*bi-l-tawāṭuʾ*), whereas the generality of righteous deeds is predicated of it by gradation (*bi-l-tashakkuk*). This indicates that the absence of loss from them is measured in proportion to the righteous deeds they performed, and there are many degrees in that.

The exception of those who believed and did righteous deeds from being in loss shows that the cause of the rest of humanity being in loss is the absence of faith and righteous deed, by the indication of the implication of the attribute (*mafhūm al-ṣifa*). It is known from the relative clause that faith and righteous deed are the cause of the absence of loss enveloping a person.

This is the conjunction of the particular to the general, for the sake of emphasis on it.
